title: Anna Maria Schwägelin Executed: Last Witchcraft Execution in German Lands
description: Anna Maria Schwägelin was executed in Kempten (in Swabia, now Bavaria) on April 11, 1775, in what is generally considered the last execution for witchcraft in the German-speaking lands. Schwägelin was a mentally unstable woman who had confessed to a pact with the devil and was convicted by a local court; her execution occurred despite the broader Enlightenment movement against witchcraft prosecution and after the Holy Roman Emperor Joseph II had ordered executions stopped in many territories. The Kempten case illustrates how witchcraft prosecution persisted in peripheral jurisdictions even as central authority moved against it, and how mental illness could lead to voluntary self-incriminating confessions outside of torture contexts.
historiographical_note: Wolfgang Behringer's Witches and Witch-Hunts (2004) discusses the late German executions including Kempten as examples of how the abolition of prosecution was uneven across European territories. The existence of Enlightenment critique did not automatically end prosecution in all areas — local authority, religious culture, and the specific circumstances of individual cases continued to produce executions into the late eighteenth century.
source_method: Kempten court records; Behringer, Witches and Witch-Hunts (2004); secondary scholarship on the decline of European witch prosecution
